title: Riemann rectangles and convergence: how does the sum approach the integral?
summary: Rectangles under a curve approximate its integral. A second panel plots the error against the number of rectangles on log-log axes, where a straight line of slope -p means the error shrinks like n to the power -p.

media.alt: Left: eight teal rectangles under a blue curve with the text n = 8, S_n = 5.351, integral = 5.500. Right: three descending straight lines on log-log axes for left, midpoint and trapezoid rules, labelled with slopes -1.18, -2.04 and -2.03, and an orange ring marking n = 8 on the left-rule line.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How does the sum approach the integral?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x from 0 to pi, y = f(x) = sin x + 0.2x + 0.8 from 0 to 2.9. Right: n (number of rectangles) from 1 to 1000 on a log axis, absolute error |S_n - integral| on a log axis from 1e-6 to 1e1; one line per rule.
look_at: On the left, are the rectangle tops above or below the curve, and do the errors cancel?
On the right, which rule's line is steepest? Steeper means faster convergence.
What does the orange ring tell you about n = 8?
Is the printed slope for the left rule exactly -1? Why or why not?
as_drawn: n = 8, S_n = 5.351 and the integral 5.500 are printed in the left panel. The exact value is 5.5002; the error is -0.149.

Legend slopes: left -1.18, midpoint -2.04, trapezoid -2.03, fitted over the first ten sample sizes (n up to about 60). The left rule's true asymptotic slope is -1 (-1.004 for n beyond 100); the printed -1.18 is a pre-asymptotic fit.
The x axis shows n, not the cost; the three rules need nearly the same number of function evaluations.
read_the_figure.proves: That the three rules converge at the orders shown, for this smooth function. It does not prove the same orders for functions with a singularity, a kink or high oscillation.
if_wrong: No n printed: the picture cannot be reproduced.
Error plotted on a linear axis: all lines look like a collapse to zero and orders cannot be read.
Fit range not stated: the slope printed depends on it.

terms.meaning: The sum of rectangle areas f(x_i) times width; it approximates the integral.
Ways to choose the height of each strip: left edge, centre, or the average of both edges.
The width of each strip, h = (b - a)/n.
The exponent p in error proportional to h^p. Doubling n divides the error by 2^p.
The slope of the error line, which equals minus the order.
The size of the difference from the exact value, without sign.

remember: Error ~ C n^(-p): a straight line of slope -p on log-log axes.
Left and right rules are first order; midpoint and trapezoid are second order.
Slope is only trustworthy once n is large enough (asymptotic range).
Print n and say which points were fitted.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: rectangles are area marks, the curve a line; text gives n and the numbers. Right: each rule is a line with its own marker and dash; position encodes n and error on logarithmic axes. The orange ring links the two panels by marking n = 8.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: An integral is an area, so rectangles show what is being approximated. The approach to the integral is a convergence question, answered in a different space: error against n. On log-log axes error equal to C n^(-p) becomes a straight line with slope -p, so the order of a method, a number that governs cost, is read from the slope and compared across rules by eye.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The slope depends on the range of n used for the fit: the render prints -1.18 for the left rule although the true order is 1. Absolute error hides whether the sum is high or low. Round-off flattens a log-log line at about 1e-16 if n is pushed far enough. A smooth test function flatters the rules; a kink or singularity lowers the order.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Printing n makes the left picture reproducible. The log-log error panel with a printed slope turns a visual impression of speed into a number. This render has both and marks the n = 8 point on the error curve, which ties the pictures together.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot error against the number of function evaluations to compare cost fairly. A convergence table with observed order between successive n is more precise than a fitted slope. For an unknown integral use Richardson extrapolation or an adaptive rule and plot the nodes chosen.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a dashed line of slope -1 and one of slope -2 as references, and compute the observed order between successive n (error ratios), shown as a small table or step plot.

steps.title: Leading error terms (Euler-Maclaurin)
steps.note: For f = sin x + 0.2x + 0.8 on [0, pi], f(b) - f(a) = 0.628 and f'(b) - f'(a) = -2. At n = 8 (h = 0.393): left predicted -0.123 against -0.149 measured; midpoint +0.01285 against +0.01291; trapezoid -0.02570 against -0.02577. The left rule's next term is O(h^2), which is why n = 8 is not yet asymptotic.

steps.title: How many rectangles for an error of 1e-4?
steps.note: The midpoint rule needs about a hundred times fewer strips than the left rule for the same accuracy.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what is the error at n = 8 for the left rule? (2) What are the orders of the three rules? (3) Roughly how many strips would the midpoint rule need to reach an error of 1e-4?

solution.text: 5.351 - 5.500 = -0.149, so the left sum is too low; the orange ring on the left line sits at about 0.15.
The magnitudes of the printed slopes: left about 1 (the -1.18 includes pre-asymptotic data), midpoint and trapezoid about 2.
The midpoint error is about 0.8 / n^2 (it is 1.3e-2 at n = 8), so 1e-4 needs n about 90.

worked.answer: Error -0.149 at n = 8; orders 1, 2, 2; the midpoint rule reaches 1e-4 with about 90 strips, the left rule needs about 10,000.

checks.q: What does a straight line of slope -2 on the error plot mean?
checks.hint: Error proportional to n to a power.
checks.answer: The error falls like n^-2: doubling the number of rectangles cuts the error by four.

checks.q: A rule's error is 1e-3 at n = 50 and 2.5e-4 at n = 100. What is its order?
Why can the fitted slope of a log-log line mislead even if the line looks straight?
checks.hint: Which points were used and how large is n?
checks.answer: Because the pre-asymptotic range has curvature and the fit depends on the n range, noise, and round-off; the true order is the slope for large n and before round-off dominates.
